title: Linux Command Cheat Sheet
markdown:
# Linux Command Cheat Sheet

A one-page reminder. Each command has a full entry in the Commands library.

## Moving around

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Where am I? | `pwd` |
| List with details, including hidden | `ls -la` |
| Go home / back / up | `cd ~` · `cd -` · `cd ..` |
| Find files by name | `find . -name "*.conf"` |

## Looking at files

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Page through a file | `less file` (q to quit) |
| First / last 20 lines | `head -n 20 file` · `tail -n 20 file` |
| Watch a log grow | `tail -f file` |
| What kind of file is it? | `file mystery` |

## Searching and shaping text

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Lines containing a word | `grep -rn "word" dir/` |
| Count lines | `wc -l file` |
| Most frequent values | `sort file \| uniq -c \| sort -nr \| head` |
| Second column of a CSV | `cut -d, -f2 data.csv` |

## Permissions and users

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Who am I? | `id` |
| Make a script executable | `chmod +x script.sh` |
| Private key permissions | `chmod 600 key` |
| What can I run as root? | `sudo -l` |

> [!WARNING]
> `rm` has no undo. Preview with `ls` first, and prefer `rm -i` while learning.

title: Common Ports and Protocols
markdown:
# Common Ports and Protocols

Defaults only: any service can listen on any port.

| Port | Protocol | Service |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 20, 21 | TCP | FTP (data, control) |
| 22 | TCP | SSH, SCP, SFTP |
| 23 | TCP | Telnet (unencrypted) |
| 25 | TCP | SMTP (mail between servers) |
| 53 | UDP/TCP | DNS |
| 67, 68 | UDP | DHCP (server, client) |
| 80 | TCP | HTTP |
| 110 | TCP | POP3 |
| 123 | UDP | NTP |
| 143 | TCP | IMAP |
| 161 | UDP | SNMP |
| 389 | TCP/UDP | LDAP |
| 443 | TCP | HTTPS |
| 445 | TCP | SMB (Windows file sharing) |
| 587 | TCP | SMTP submission (mail clients) |
| 993 | TCP | IMAPS |
| 995 | TCP | POP3S |
| 1433 | TCP | Microsoft SQL Server |
| 3306 | TCP | MySQL / MariaDB |
| 3389 | TCP | RDP (Windows Remote Desktop) |
| 5432 | TCP | PostgreSQL |
| 5900 | TCP | VNC |
| 6379 | TCP | Redis |
| 8080 | TCP | Alternate HTTP (proxies, dev servers) |

## Checking a port

- Is something listening here? `ss -tulpn` (Linux)
- Is that port reachable? `nc -zv host 443`
- What is running on it? `nmap -sV -p 443 host` (only against systems you may test)

title: SSH Quick Guide
markdown:
# SSH Quick Guide

## Make a key pair

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "lab laptop"
```

Accept the default location and set a passphrase. This creates `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (private, never share) and `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` (public).

## Install the public key on a server

```bash
ssh-copy-id student@192.0.2.10
```

## Permissions SSH insists on

```bash
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```

## A tidy `~/.ssh/config`

```text
Host lab
  HostName 192.0.2.10
  User student
  Port 22
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```

Then `ssh lab` is enough.

## Tunnels

| Goal | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Reach a remote web server locally | `ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 lab` then open http://localhost:8080 |
| SOCKS proxy through the host | `ssh -D 1080 -N lab` |
| Go through a jump host | `ssh -J jump@198.51.100.5 student@10.0.0.7` |

> [!TIP]
> On first connection compare the host key fingerprint with one you trust. A changed key later means a rebuilt server, or someone in the middle.

Related: [[cmd:ssh]], [[cmd:scp]], [[File Permissions]].

title: Local DNS and the hosts file
markdown:
# Local DNS and the hosts file

The hosts file maps names to addresses on one machine and is consulted before DNS. Handy for lab setups (`web.lab.test` pointing at a VM) and for testing.

## Where it lives

| System | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Linux, macOS | `/etc/hosts` |
| Windows | `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` |

Editing needs administrator rights (`sudo` on Linux/macOS, an elevated editor on Windows).

## Add an entry

```text
192.0.2.10   web.lab.test
```

One address, then one or more names, separated by spaces.

## Flush the DNS cache after changes

| System | Command |
| --- | --- |
| macOS | `sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder` |
| Windows | `ipconfig /flushdns` |
| Linux (systemd-resolved) | `resolvectl flush-caches` |

## Check it

```bash
ping -c 1 web.lab.test
dig +short web.lab.test      # asks DNS, so it will NOT show hosts-file entries
```

> [!NOTE]
> `dig` talks to DNS servers directly and ignores the hosts file; `ping` and browsers use the system resolver, which reads it.

Related: [[DNS (Domain Name System)]], [[cmd:dig]].
